label: Yehoshua (Joshua) — Part 1 — Chapters 1–8
summary_plain: After Moshe's death, YHWH speaks to Yehoshua: Be strong and courageous. Do not be frightened. YHWH your Creator is with you wherever you go. Yehoshua sends spies to Yericho. Rachav the innkeeper hides them and declares: YHWH your Creator — he is Creator in the heavens above and on the earth beneath. Yisra'EL crosses the Yarden on dry ground. They take twelve stones from the river. They circumcise the new generation at Gilgal. The commander of YHWH's army appears to Yehoshua. Yericho falls when the people shout. Ai is taken after Akhan's sin is purged.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads from DSS Joshua fragments (4QJosh-a, 4QJosh-b) and the Orit Ge'ez. The Yehoshua narrative is the fulfillment of the land promise in Bereshit 15. The crossing of the Yarden parallels the crossing of the sea in Shemot 14. The twelve stones mark the covenant community's entry into the promised territory — physically African soil on the Nubian tectonic plate west of the Jordan Rift Valley.

key_terms.definition: Successor to Mosheh, leader of Yisra'el's entry into Kena'an. YHWH's command at the opening of the book: 'Be strong and courageous — do not be afraid.' Yehoshua led the Jordan crossing, the Jericho campaign, and the initial conquest. His name means 'YHWH saves.'

In Yehoshua 3-4, YHWH stops the Jordan's flow as the priests carrying the Ark step into the water. The entire nation crosses on dry ground — a deliberate parallel to the Red Sea crossing. Twelve stones are set up at Gilgal as a memorial. The generation that did not witness the Red Sea now witnesses its own miracle.

The woman in Yeriho who hides the two Israelite spies and secures a promise of protection for her family. She signals with a scarlet cord in her window. When Yeriho falls, Rahav and her household are spared. She is a Kenaanite woman whose faith-action saves her — a critical figure in the Yeriho narrative.

The first city conquered in Kena'an. YHWH's command: march around the city once daily for six days, seven times on the seventh day, then blow the trumpets and shout. The walls collapse. Yeriho is placed under total Kherem (devoted destruction) — no plunder taken. Akhan's violation of the Kherem is the central crisis of chapter 7.

Devoted destruction — the total consecration of conquered peoples and goods to YHWH, with nothing kept for personal use. In Yeriho, the entire city and its contents are Kherem. The only exception is Rahav's household (protected by covenant promise) and the silver, gold, and bronze vessels (brought to YHWH's treasury). Kherem is not ordinary war-plunder — it is a covenant act.

The Israelite man from the tribe of Yehudah who secretly took a Babylonian garment, silver, and gold from the Kherem of Yeriho. His violation caused the defeat at Ai. When exposed by lot and confession, Akhan and his household are executed in the Valley of Akhor. The name 'Akhor' (trouble) becomes a place-name memorial.

The second city targeted after Yeriho. The first attempt is routed because of Akhan's hidden sin — the Kherem has been violated. After Akhan is executed, Yehoshua uses a military ambush strategy (feigned retreat) and destroys Ai. The contrast between Yeriho (miraculous wall-collapse) and Ai (tactical ambush) shows YHWH working through both supernatural and tactical means.

The first campsite in Kena'an, near Yeriho, where the Jordan memorial stones are set up and where the generation born in the wilderness is circumcised. Gilgal becomes the base of operations for the initial campaign. Circumcision at Gilgal 'rolled away the reproach of Mitzrayim' — restoring the covenant sign to the generation that grew up without it.

In Yehoshua 8:30-35, after the Ai campaign, Yehoshua builds an altar on Mount Eival and reads all the Torah — blessings and curses — to the entire assembly. This follows Mosheh's command in Devarim 27. The covenant is renewed publicly, with the entire nation present, women and children and strangers included.

In Yehoshua 2, Yehoshua sends two spies into Yeriho before the crossing. They are hidden by Rahav and escape via a rope through her window. Their report to Yehoshua is the opposite of the Qadesh-Barnea spies: 'YHWH has given all the land into our hands, and all the inhabitants are melting in fear of us.' Faith against fear.

faq.question: How does Yehoshua's opening connect to Mosheh's death at the end of Devarim?
faq.answer: Yehoshua opens immediately after Mosheh's death: 'After the death of Mosheh the servant of YHWH, YHWH spoke to Yehoshua.' There is no gap — the covenant leadership transfers without interruption. YHWH's commission to Yehoshua directly parallels what was said to Mosheh: 'Be strong and courageous.' The Torah promises made to Avraham, Yitzhak, and Ya'akov are now being fulfilled. Yehoshua's first task is not military planning but immersion in the Torah: 'Meditate on the Book of the Torah day and night.' Covenant fidelity comes before military strategy.

faq.question: Why is Rahav significant?
faq.answer: Rahav is a Kenaanite woman — not an Israelite — who acts with greater faith than many in Yisra'el. She hides the spies, deceives the king of Yeriho, and negotiates covenant protection for her family. Her declaration to the spies is theologically precise: 'YHWH your Creator is the Creator in heaven above and on the earth below.' This is the Shema's core claim, stated by an outsider. Rahav is preserved and her household is spared — the promise is kept. Her scarlet cord becomes the sign of covenant protection, echoing the blood on the doorposts at the first Passover.

faq.question: Why is the Jordan crossing structured as a parallel to the Red Sea crossing?
faq.answer: The Jordan crossing in Yehoshua 3-4 deliberately mirrors the Red Sea crossing in Shemot 14: both involve water being stopped by YHWH's power, both create dry ground for the people to cross, and both are covenant demonstrations that YHWH fights for Yisra'el. The difference: at the Red Sea the people were fleeing; at the Jordan they are advancing. The covenant generation that grew up in the wilderness needed to witness their own founding miracle. The twelve stones at Gilgal serve the same function as the song of the sea — a memorial that future generations will ask about and be told the answer.

faq.question: What is Kherem and why does Akhan's violation matter so much?
faq.answer: Kherem is total consecration — devoted destruction. When YHWH commands Kherem, every living thing and every valuable is YHWH's; nothing may be taken for private use. The Yeriho Kherem was explicit. Akhan's violation was not an accident or a minor theft — it was treating YHWH's property as his own and hiding it. The covenant consequence is corporate: all of Yisra'el is affected by one person's hidden sin. This is the covenant's communal accountability principle — the community is one body, and hidden transgression poisons the whole. The public exposure and execution at Akhor is a covenant surgery removing the contamination.

faq.question: What is the significance of the covenant renewal at Mount Eival?
faq.answer: Mosheh had commanded in Devarim 27 that when Yisra'el entered the land, they should build an altar on Mount Eival and read the Torah — blessings and curses — to the entire assembly. Yehoshua does exactly this in 8:30-35: immediately after the Ai campaign, with the land barely secured, the entire nation assembles for covenant renewal. The timing matters: the first order of business in the land is covenant recommitment, not further military conquest. And the reading is comprehensive: 'not a word of all that Mosheh commanded was omitted.' The entry into the land is a covenant ceremony, not primarily a military campaign.

faq.question: What is the contrast between the Qadesh-Barnea spies and the Yeriho spies?
faq.answer: In Bamidbar 13-14 (Qadesh-Barnea), ten of twelve spies brought back a report of fear — 'we were like grasshoppers in our own sight.' That failure cost the entire generation their entry into the land. In Yehoshua 2, the two spies return from Yeriho with a completely different report: 'YHWH has given all the land — all the inhabitants are melting in fear of us.' Same land, different generation, different faith. The contrast is deliberate: the wilderness period produced a generation capable of the trust that the previous generation failed. Kalev and Yehoshua — the two faithful Qadesh-Barnea spies — are still present, now leading.

faq.question: How is the fall of Yeriho different from the conquest of Ai?
faq.answer: Yeriho falls through direct divine action — no siege machines, no military strategy, just marching, trumpets, and shouting. YHWH gives the city. Ai is different: after the Akhan contamination is removed, Yehoshua uses a tactical ambush — a feigned retreat to draw out Ai's defenders while a hidden force takes the city from behind. YHWH gives the victory but through military strategy. The two campaigns together show YHWH working through both supernatural intervention and human tactical wisdom. Neither approach is more 'holy' than the other — both operate under YHWH's command.

faq.question: What is Gilgal's theological significance in the first chapters of Yehoshua?
faq.answer: Gilgal is the first campsite in Kena'an and the base of operations for the initial campaign. Three covenant events happen there: the Jordan memorial stones are erected (covenant memory), the wilderness generation is circumcised (covenant sign restored), and the first Passover in the land is celebrated (covenant calendar kept). YHWH declares at Gilgal: 'Today I have rolled away the reproach of Mitzrayim.' The name Gilgal is linked to the Hebrew root for 'rolling' (galal). Gilgal is the threshold point — where Yisra'el becomes fully covenant-active in the land, not merely in transit.

faq.question: What is the significance of Yehoshua 1:8 — meditating on the Torah day and night?
faq.answer: YHWH's first instruction to Yehoshua before any military action: 'The Book of the Torah shall not depart from your mouth. You shall meditate on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do all that is written in it.' Military success is explicitly tied to Torah fidelity. This reverses the conventional expectation that a military commander needs tactical training above all. Yehoshua's strength comes from covenant obedience, not martial skill. The Qumran community found this framework directly applicable to their own situation: covenant fidelity in the wilderness is the preparation for YHWH's victory, not human force.

faq.question: Who are the two spies Yehoshua sends and what is their mission?
faq.answer: The book does not name the two spies. Their mission: reconnaissance of Yeriho — specifically to understand its defenses and the population's morale. They are hidden by Rahav and escape via rope through her window. The mission produces intelligence about morale (everyone is terrified) and establishes the covenant promise to Rahav. The un-named spies contrast with the twelve named spies of Bamidbar 13 — the emphasis is on their function (faithful reconnaissance resulting in a confident report) rather than their individual identity. Their faith produces a positive report; the named Qadesh-Barnea majority produced a faithless one.
